Therefore, these ten realms do not transcend a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), as is clearly explained in the extensive exposition of the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*).
Furthermore, the reason the previous explanation regarding the Śākyas did not employ the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) was for the sake of clarifying the meaning of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

These three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth are also the three virtues; since they already possess the sense of "lineage" (*gotra*), there is no need to rely on the previous [explanation]. As for the application of the realms, it is more convenient to do so; thus, within the ten realms, one discusses the differences and non-differences between Buddhas and ordinary beings, or in relation to the three truths (*tisatya*).

Next, regarding the principle that "the three dharmas are themselves the three types of wisdom," the reason the term "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is used at the beginning of each of the three stages is that mindfulness takes the object as its domain; the same applies to reflection (*cintā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Thus, the "objects" refer to what is heard, what is reflected upon, and what is cultivated.
The phrase "all say 'what'" refers to the objects of apprehension. The term "that which is contemplated" and so forth indicates the four dharmas explained in the lower teachings;

according to these teachings, there are differences in reflection (*cintā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Regarding the objects within the realms, there are variations in their quantity and reduction; one should understand that the skillfulness or clumsiness of the contemplative essence follows the meaning [of the teaching]. These distinctions and non-distinctions are established by contrasting the provisional with the real.

Regarding the initial mention of "function" (*yòng*): there must be wisdom that apprehends an object for there to be that which is apprehended; since this cites a concrete instance to manifest wisdom, it is called "function.
What is termed "essence" (*tǐ*) refers to the entity itself.

Within the objective sphere (*viṣaya*), each phenomenon is that which is apprehended (*grāhya*); since mindfulness and the others precede [the apprehension], they first apprehend the phenomena that are to be apprehended.
Now, by first asking "How? (*kathaṃ*), one points to the essence of the mindful subject; the same applies to reflection (*cintā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Therefore, one should know that these are the very essence of the three types of wisdom; this essence is precisely that which is able to hear, contemplate, and cultivate. Thus, it is said: "to record the dharmas heard, and so forth."

Regarding the term "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*): it refers to that by which one must hear the teachings; mindfulness and so forth are precisely what constitutes the capacity to hear and so on.

It is not through the distinction of the subject who grasps that they become separate characteristics, but rather through the differences in the teachings heard—divided into the five vehicles and seven types of goodness—that the union of subject and object constitutes the causes and conditions for hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

Regarding the statement, "Taking the apprehension of objects and hearing the Dharma as causes and conditions": both the apprehended object and the apprehending subject are termed the cause, while hearing the Dharma serves as the condition for the arising of wisdom; this wisdom is the dharma that is produced.

Furthermore, regarding "grasping the object": grasping an object must take hearing the Dharma as its cause. Since this is first indicated, the three objects serve as the cause and hearing the Dharma serves as the condition; thus, although there is initially hearing and so forth, one further requires hearing the Dharma to serve as a wholesome condition. Therefore, it is called "cause and condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
One should know that although the objects, essences, and causal conditions of the three types of wisdom are threefold, they are in fact twofold.

To explain the causal conditions again by combining them with the preceding objects and essences: the essence is itself wisdom; the object must derive its name from the essence, and the essence must establish its designation through the object.

Regarding the "further explanation of causes and conditions": this refers to the fact that one has already added the hearing of the Dharma to prevent the conceptualizations of self and other, and has established mutual causes and conditions;
only when these three meanings are fully present do wisdom and its intended purpose come to fruition.
Regarding the phrase "these three vehicles" and so forth: the five [categories] exclude humans and devas, because the vehicle of humans and devas is not yet termed "wisdom.
Question:
Previously it was said there are ten realms; why is it stated here that there are only three vehicles?
Answer: Although they differ in being extensive or concise, their underlying principle is one and the same.
However, while the "seeds" (bīja) are universal, the "vehicles" (yāna) are specific; because the Great Vehicle is integrated and the Small Vehicle is expanded, there are only three vehicles.

Furthermore, the four factors beginning with "seeds" necessarily pervade the ten realms; within these, the arising of wisdom is necessarily restricted to the three vehicles, because the three vehicles are common to all four realms.

Regarding the phrase "the causes of the five vehicles," wisdom is necessarily restricted to the three [vehicles], while cause and effect together encompass the five; the principle for excluding the other seven [factors] can be understood by analogy with the preceding explanation.

As for not mentioning the "four arisings," this is merely following the ascent and emergence [of the text]. Master Daosheng fully elaborates upon the methods of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation through the various *pāramitās* and other dharmas; however, he has not yet differentiated the six *pāramitās* according to the three vehicles. Thus, while the six are universal and pervasive, the three encompass the six.

Regarding the phrase "this refers to a single dharma": among the four meanings, the first three concern the capacity that distinguishes the object; this [fourth] concerns the discourse on the object based on that capacity. Since there is no differentiation within the object, it is a single dharma. Therefore, according to the first three meanings, the Tathāgata possesses a single dharma without differentiation; however, these are merely presented in contrast to the capacity for cognition by way of their objects.
Regarding the phrase "without distinction" followed by "and so forth," this merely refers to the distinctions and non-distinctions as previously detailed.
As for "the immeasurable within the one," the intended meaning is simply the immeasurability of a single family (or school).

Within each and every virtue, one may distinguish immeasurable conditions; as it is said, "many names," and so forth—one should understand that within the immeasurable, a single instance follows this same principle.
"What is it? This introduces a brief distinction regarding what is excluded. What is it?

Since the followers of the Two Vehicles also possess this, and since both have detached from attachment and entered into quiescence, their names are the same while their essences differ; therefore, it is explained again by means of contrast.

Regarding the phrase "perpetually quiescent" (*nitya-śānta*) and so forth, it further uses non-differentiation to conclude that the distinctions between the two vehicles ultimately return to emptiness; this may be understood by analogy with other cases.
As for the expression "earnestly clapping the hands," *di* (抵) means "to strike"; it refers to the hands striking against the palms to express diligent effort.

Having already explained this above, I now explain it again because this matter is not easy; thus I have applied diligent effort repeatedly. This was so even during the Buddha’s own lifetime, how much more so in the final age.

Regarding the passage from "Refuting the Old" to "If the Buddha, etc.," the ancients used this to explain the [Buddha’s] limited lifespan (āyus-pramāṇa), thereby missing the essential meaning all the more severely. Now, using this same passage to explain the teaching of eternal abiding (nityatva), I call it the "Suffering Sūtra";
since it is neither born nor extinguished, yet they speak of it as being "intermittent and severed," I call it the "Suffering Buddha."
The Sūtra states that the Buddha has no suffering; it is those who impose [suffering] upon him who are at fault. Thus, he is merely called "the Buddha of Suffering" and so forth.

Guangzhai’s notion of "having a remainder" (youyu) is insufficient to distinguish this difference. Nevertheless, in all of Guangzhai’s writings, he refutes the Bodhisattva of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* without understanding what is being addressed; here, he simply uses the Mahāyāna term "having a remainder" to explain away ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).

As for the phrase "there is a person" who departs, others find it difficult to accept this interpretation at Guangzhai Monastery; even among the ancients, there were those who did not permit this explanation, let alone our Master of today.
Below the section on the "scriptural text," our Master provides the correct interpretation.
There is indeed a sound reason for the previous re-explanation in contrast to the Two Vehicles.
While it may be acceptable to proceed in this manner for the time being by citing various past commentaries to challenge Guangzhai’s views,
one still fails to understand how the "emptiness of the primary meaning" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) of the old [tradition] differs from that of the Lesser Vehicle.

Regarding "following the three *siddhis*," the One Reality is likewise taken as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); in contrast to the provisional, there are three, which refers to following desires and complying with provisional capacities in the past.

Next, regarding the refutation of doubts through the core doctrine: the phrase "although not yet" acknowledges [the disciples] as being of the same class; once they have received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), they are immediately true Buddhas. From the Deer Park onwards, they have fully mastered both the provisional and the real; reaching the stage of *amṛta* (the finest essence), their mastery of the karma is not in vain. One should know that the previous praise of Śākyamuni was originally intended to extol what Kāśyapa has mastered.

Regarding the "Dispelling of Doubts": it is feared that at this time, the assembly, hearing the Buddha describe what they themselves had not yet mastered, might fail to understand the Buddha’s intent and instead claim that Kāśyapa’s mastery was inadequate. Therefore, [the Buddha] describes his own provisional and ultimate teachings to praise Kāśyapa’s ability to know the Tathāgata’s preaching according to suitability, noting that although he himself has mastered the ultimate reality, it simultaneously encompasses all things.
Question:
Why is "investigating doubt" (*tanyu*) not explained? Answer:

In the teachings of the Shared Vehicle (Śrāvakayāna), the manifest and the hidden, as well as the real and the provisional, are easily distinguished; therefore, the Buddha provisionally described and praised [the Dharma] according to these teachings.
If that is so, then the "exploring" [of the ultimate] is most questionable—why would it apply exclusively to the teachings of the Shared Vehicle?
Answer:

Although difficult, it is easy; for when the assembly hears the teaching on the Tathāgata’s two types of wisdom, they realize that the Buddha’s Dharma-body constantly contemplates both the great and the small. Fearing that their understanding of the teachings might not be entirely correct, the Buddha thus describes his two teachings and two types of wisdom to show that his uniform instruction is free from error.
Furthermore, since even the exposition of the *Ji* (the *Zhengyi jing*) is itself not empty of meaning, we can verify that the insights and understandings [of the author] are likewise not erroneous.

Regarding the "Explanation of the Intent of the Exposition": previously, one just dismissed what was understood as being insufficient; how could one now, in this context, suddenly claim that what was understood is truly rare?
Therefore, we know that the preceding passage merely records the Tathāgata’s own account of his capacity for knowledge; what concern does it have with Kāśyapa?
Thus, the present commentary explains:

although the World-Honored One recounts this himself, in principle Kāśyapa should have received all of it. Since Kāśyapa has personally received it from beginning to end, and since it likewise traverses the provisional and the real across the five periods, its meaning encompasses everything; therefore, he too is worthy of praise as being most rare and extraordinary.

However, Zhan’an’s re-exegesis consists merely of a commentary on the thirteen verses of the preceding chapter that praise the profundity of the Buddha’s grace; this signifies that within his own realm, he is able to know [the truth] according to what is appropriate, and that within his own realm, both phenomena and principle encompass everything.
Question:
In this context, the preceding praise of the Buddha’s profound kindness—how does it differ from that of the ancients? Answer:

The ancients simply spoke of "profound gratitude" without distinguishing whether that gratitude was recent or long-standing; therefore, previously, thirteen verses were used to fully encompass the beginning and end, whereas now, the Buddha provides a detailed account, which is what constitutes a "recounted fulfillment."
This is Zhiyi’s (Zhang’an) assistance in clarifying his vision, which, based on the Great Master’s intent, naturally achieves profound significance.

Regarding the phrase "How could there be," etc., it refers to Kāśyapa and others as a single type of capacity (*eka-yogya*) and points to this Sahā world as a single realm; because other capacities do not comprehend it, it is said that "words cannot exhaust its expression."

Regarding Kāśyapa and the other four, although the preceding chapter merely spoke of the "Great Benevolence of the Tathāgata," since the Tathāgata has already remotely observed that Kāśyapa was able to both receive and comprehend the two [teachings], how could he not know the initial fourfold great grace? This extends even to his final commissioning of me to transform others; the ritual protocols throughout the ten directions do not exceed this. Therefore, it is now described here in full through both prose and verse, such that the three types of grass and two types of trees, all sharing one earth and one rain, completely recount the beginning and end of Kāśyapa’s realization.

Regarding the phrase "the wealth of body, mind, and Dharma": it means that the body has received the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) and the mind has attained the wealth of the Dharma, having already realized the seat of ultimate truth—the single reality of emptiness.

If one relies on this meaning, the Buddha originally recounted the beginning and end of Kāśyapa’s life in detail; however, because the assembly did not understand it at the time, it was necessary to remove their doubts. Therefore, the commentary explains: "Kāśyapa was able to know."
If one investigates this intent, how can it be said that the four hidden objections are identical to this?
If this were not the case, what would be the purpose of the words of great kindness?

To describe one's gratitude incompletely results in a betrayal of righteousness; if one were to give rise [to such thoughts], one would surely reproach oneself. Why, then, does the Buddha praise those who are able to believe and accept?
Furthermore, in the subsequent verse, only the detailed [teaching] is versified rather than the abbreviated, because the detailed encompasses the abbreviated.
Next, regarding the section "Those with Wisdom" and below, which concerns those with provisional wisdom: Question:
Since it says "if those with wisdom hear it," this must pertain to the capacity [of the listener]; how can it pertain to the Buddha?
Answer: If it were not spoken by one possessing wisdom, how could it cause those possessing wisdom to have faith?

Regarding the statement, "All that prior to this is called 'erroneous,'" for Kāśyapa and the other four, their views prior to hearing this analogy would indeed constitute wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), as their vision had not yet been rectified. Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* separately cites the account of the youth Kāśyapa’s own description as an illustration; he too, prior to hearing the *Nirvāṇa*, referred to himself as holding wrong view.

Regarding the passage from "the Response Body" (nirmāṇakāya) to "containing moisture": all words spoken in the teaching of the Dharma pertain to the Response Body; therefore, both superior and inferior responses are the articulation of the bodily and vocal karma of the Form Body (rūpakāya). As for the new scriptures, which identify the Enjoyment Body for Others (parasaṃbhogakāya) as Vairocana—since this is still not the Self-Enjoyment Body (svasaṃbhogakāya), would it not be taught [as such]?
If you claim that the essence is identical [to the response-body], then all ten bodies are equally identical; why then speak of the response-body alone?

One might as well say that the three bodies are identical, such that speech and silence are no different; how can one discard the six-foot body—the partial honored form—and focus only on the ocean of marks, as if space were merely flowers and there were no space outside the flowers?

Regarding the phrase "capable of possessing" and so forth: it is therefore known that the partial and limited scriptures of the past did not bestow or reveal the rain of the Buddha-nature—which is perfect and eternal—contained within the twelve divisions of the canon; thus, the clouds did not hold moisture.
Although it is stated in the first two [types of] moisture that there is no "receiving," this does not mean they lack the sense of "pervasion" or possess the quality of "moistening.
As for the statement, "The Buddha Susīma did not preach the Dharma," this refers to the *Mahāśāstra* text, which takes the total absence of preaching as the meaning of "not containing [the Dharma]."
Prabhūtaratna does not speak of this; the meaning is as explained in the subsequent text.
Regarding the ninety-eight *anuśayas*: when one first severs the afflictions of views and craving, one attains the benefit of the True Truth (*satyārtha*).
As for the statement "coolness on the stages" (*bhūmi*), even the stage of the purification of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*) is provisionally excluded from this.

Regarding the passage from "The hundred grains and the language-communication" to "the hundred virtues": each of the five vehicles takes the hundred virtues as its foundation. As for the term "capable of producing," this is stated from the perspective of the fruit;

if stated from the perspective of the cause, it is that the hundred virtues produce the five vehicles. Since how could the causes of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna exceed the ten wholesome actions? Therefore, the ten wholesome actions are mutually adorned with one another.
As for the statement, "If one cannot cultivate the causes for mutual adornment," this is not being discussed here.
If that were so, there would be no hundred [of such] human vehicles. Answer:
Wine obstructs the ground of the mind; it is not incorrect to speak of this in general terms. Regarding the phrase "sugarcane" and so forth:

since two substances are mentioned, there must be a corresponding pairing. Let us now attempt to pair them: the single substance of sugarcane can be used as a metaphor for concentration (*samādhi*), while the manifold forms of grapevines can be used as a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*). Wisdom is categorized according to what it eliminates, whereas concentration is categorized according to its object; thus, they are distinguished by being manifold and singular, respectively.

Regarding the phrase "Having already set forth the ten titles in the three lines of verse below," the text is concise while the meaning is complete: "transcending the world" (*lokottara*) refers to both the "Unsurpassed One" (*anuttarapuruṣa*) and the "Buddha.
"Yu" (于) means "in" or "at."
He is described as the Truly and Fully Enlightened One (*samyaksambuddha*) and the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct (*vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*), which constitute the tenth title;
among gods and humans, he is the Tamer of Men (*puruṣadamyasārathi*) and the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*); the Thus-Come One (*tathāgata*) constitutes the first title;
he who comes well and departs well is the Well-Gone One (*sugata*); furthermore, having emerged from the world, he is the Knower of the World (*lokavid*).

Regarding the "Four Great Vows" following "to fill and moisten": "filling and moistening sentient beings" corresponds to the first great vow; "causing all to be free from suffering" corresponds to the second vow; and "causing all to be free from the suffering of both cause and effect, thereby attaining peaceful and secure happiness," corresponds to the third vow.
And the bliss of nirvāṇa is the fourth vow.
All five vehicles possess worldly happiness, yet [the Buddha] causes them all to attain the supreme bliss.

Within the section on "Exhorting to Listen and Accept," there are further two parts: first, the initial two lines praise the Buddha; second, from "For the Great Assembly" onwards, it shows that because the speaker is honored, the Dharma he teaches is wondrous. Since the seven types of goodness all ultimately return to the One Vehicle, he exhorts them to listen and accept. This cites non-differentiation to explain differentiation.

Regarding the phrase "The Buddha’s teaching is impartial," etc.: because there is attachment and aversion, there arises the distinction between "self" and "other. One would not feel attachment toward those with the capacity for the Buddha's teaching while feeling aversion toward those with other capacities.

Nobility and meanness, high and low, are distinguished by rank; observing the precepts and violating them are distinguished by conduct; sharp faculties and dull faculties are distinguished by training. Furthermore, one must fully traverse the five vehicles and the seven virtues, explaining them in successive order.

Regarding the subsequent explanation of the "three types of grass and two types of trees" following the section on "those who possess persons," the ancient masters differ in their views. However, while the names for the two large trees are fixed, those for the two large grasses are not, as they are combined under a single name; whereas for the two small grasses, the Sūtra itself provides specific names, so there can be no dispute. Nevertheless, it was not yet known that there were two kinds of the Two Vehicles (dviyāna). Therefore, the first master enumerates all five stages, while the second and third masters list only three stages, because the two types of grass share the same meaning and all three [categories] have not yet attained their respective titles.

Regarding the passage "However, as for the three types of grass," the following is now explained. First, the general refutation states: "To follow one's own mind and oppose the Buddha is to contravene the scriptures. To act without receiving the lineage of transmission is "following one's own mind" (*śī-mānasa*); for the Buddha’s intention is not thus, it is therefore "opposing the Buddha."

Regarding the phrase "contradicting the sūtra": the sūtra clarifies that the reception of moisture differs according to the distinctions among the five vehicles; how then could these three stages all be identical within a single teaching?

Regarding the "two interpretations for advancement and retreat" within the section on "receiving moisture separately": first, the sūtra text is directly interpreted; second, the example of wood is applied to grass, explaining it by analogy with the underlying principle—since there are three types of grass, wood should likewise be treated as an example.
Seeing "seeking the World-Honored One" within the passage on the great grasses, they claim it also applies to the latter [stage];
seeing "devoting the mind to the Buddha-way" within the passage on the small trees, they claim it applies to both the beginning and the end;

seeing "delivering immeasurable billions" within the passage on the great trees, they claim it applies to the preceding two. Thus, they construct a single interpretation that traverses all the stages.
In recent times, those who have abandoned the ancient sūtras, śāstras, and various teachings of the Bodhisattvas have committed a great transgression;
therefore, I shall now provide a separate commentary that remains in profound accord with the scriptural texts.

Regarding the phrase "the superior grass constitutes the six perfections": since it is stated that one practices diligence (*vīrya*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and diligence is the foremost among the six perfections, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

"Generosity, ethical discipline, and patience are the common dharmas of the world; if one wishes to cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom, one must necessarily practice diligence. Furthermore, because diligence universally enters into all five [perfections], for this reason, diligence is cited as encompassing the six. Therefore, it is not the case that the two types of wood exist only during the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

Since the *Sūtra* within the *Kṣudraka Āgama* states that one who constantly practices compassion knows for oneself that one will become a Buddha, whereas a Bodhisattva of the Six Perfections only attains certain knowledge of this at the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, the former does not apply universally. However, once one has surpassed the second bhūmi, one necessarily knows that one will become a Buddha; thus, it differs from the previous case and is designated according to its superior significance.

Since it is stated within the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta Sūtra* that one "turns the non-retrogressive wheel," and since those of the Separate Teaching (Bie) can turn the Dharma-wheel from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward—which constitutes "non-retrogression through mindfulness"—whereas those of the Treasury (Zang) and the Shared (Tong) teachings only turn the Dharma-wheel upon reaching the fruit, how could they be called "such Bodhisattvas"? Thus, we know this refers to the Separate Teaching.
Next, in order to establish the three types of wood and three types of bodhisattvas and to enable the understanding of their respective categories, this is further explained.

Thus, the opening analogy in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks of "three woods and two herbs," identifying the small herb as the common medicine and the superior herb as the supreme medicine; yet the verse text instead says "three medicines and two woods. For this reason, the present text provides both general and specific interpretations.
Regarding the explanation of "increase" (*vṛddhi*), there are two different interpretations concerning the increase of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), both of which reflect the intention of our Master.
The former interpretation holds that one is called "final" only after attaining the extinction of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) characteristic of the Small Vehicle.
Next, in the explanation of the Mahāyāna, it is only here that one is called "one in their final existence" (*paścima-bhavika*).
Both the Great and Small Vehicles are termed "growth," and this growth arises entirely from encountering a Buddha.

Sentient beings themselves claim that growth occurs within their own respective divisions; however, according to the Buddha’s intention, there is no growth apart from the rain from the clouds. Thus, even within their own divisions, there is ultimately growth, which is why it is only upon reaching this point that they realize the oneness [of the vehicles]. The statement that there is "no further [existence]" is merely a concession to the provisional teachings of the Small Vehicle; it is not that there is absolutely no [further existence] at all.

If one attains the Dharma-body and undergoes a single transformation toward equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one shall enter the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*suviśuddha-bodhi*); this is what is meant by "the final [birth]. The *Śāstra* states:

"After an Arhat has resolved their mind [for enlightenment], the power of the ultimate limit-concentration (*prāntakoṭi-dhyāna*) causes their segmented body (*paricchinna-śarīra*) to extend until it reaches the transformative body (*nirmāṇa-śarīra*). Regarding the statement that they no longer alter their retribution to achieve the unsurpassed fruit, this mostly pertains to the general meaning; for while a Bodhisattva of the general category may transcend the stages of the Two Vehicles, their delusions and the body born of moisture may either lead them to perfect enlightenment after passing through births or without passing through births at all. How could the fruit of the Flower-King Buddha utilize the body of the ultimate limit-concentration belonging to the Two Vehicles?
Therefore, one should ask:
Is this samādhi identical to or different from that Śūraṅgama-samādhi?

All treatises state that one abandons the body of分段 (paricchinna-deha) to enter the body of 變易 (nirmāṇa-deha); however, it is not necessarily so according to the intention of Vasubandhu’s commentary, though I fear his interpretation of the meaning may not be correct.
Thus we know that the statement regarding "final increase" differs for both the Great and Small Vehicles; there is no teaching among them that can serve as a profound standard.
Question:

If this is so, then the other three stages should likewise each have two interpretations: first, if one does not encounter a Buddha during these three stages, there is no increase; if one does encounter a Buddha, there is increase within those respective stages.

Second, those who, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, dwelt in the bodies of the four stages and were matured by the Buddha, only when they reach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and attain entry into the one reality are they called "increased.
Answer: However, because among the five stages the two vehicles have strong attachments and claim [their stage] to be the final one, two interpretations are required.
The other three [categories] already have clear and explicit textual evidence; this is the case throughout the entire context and meaning of the passage.
Question:
It is said that both *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* alike must see a Buddha while dwelling in their final body (*caramabhavika*). Why is it that this is not the case for *pratyekabuddhas*?
Answer: Although [the growth] occurs after the Buddha’s appearance, its fundamental cause lies in the Buddha’s era; this can be seen through reflection. Regarding the passage “growth...

and so forth” (*yunyun*) following [the mention of] "growth," it fully explains the meaning of the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as the present and past. Although the five stages themselves are called "growth," at the very inception of their sprouting, they are nothing other than earth and rain. While the teaching places earth and rain last, growth must necessarily begin with the initial sprout. Thus, what is being shown here is merely the sequence of the beginning and end of earth and rain.
One should also explain in detail the meaning of the general and specific increases.

Regarding the question, "Are the single cloud and single rain the same as or different from the single sound? the intent of the question is to ask whether the single earth and single rain are the same as or different from the teaching of the single sound.

The meaning of the response is as follows: here, the single cloud and single rain serve as distinct metaphors for the opening and revealing [of the truth]. That teaching of the single voice applies universally to both cause and effect, as well as to the partial and the perfect; herein, we first distinguish between cause and effect, and subsequently analyze the partial and the perfect.

Although the distinction between cause and effect in the preceding section was intended in that way, it nonetheless followed the various teachings by using the metaphor of two kinds of clouds and rain to represent how the causes and effects of those teachings correspond to their respective portions within the single voice. Now, however, the question is posed from the perspective of the ultimate clouds and rain, and in the response, the two kinds of "single voice" are specifically set forth.

Regarding the term "lower stages" (*adhobhūmi*): it may refer to the six sense organs of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), or to the stages prior to the grounds (*diqian*) of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). If it refers to the stages from the first abode (*prathamavihāra*) up to, but not including, Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), how could it be that there is no single sound according to the species (*yulei yiyin*) at all?
Next, in the analysis of the partial and the perfect, first the errors of previous [scholars] are presented; then, within the correct interpretation, there are three parts:
first the perfect, second the partial, and finally the clarification of one's own retribution.
Regarding the citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* within the section on the perfect, it serves to refute the three aforementioned masters.
What is called "retribution" (or "response") refers to a reply.
This single sound likewise reaches those in the lower realms, yet it does not engage their six sense faculties.

Next, regarding the term "Vibhāṣā," this is cited as an instance of the partial being used to illustrate the perfect; though the categories are intended to be the same, it remains merely the single sound of the Buddha within the Tripiṭaka teachings.
If this were not the case, would you be able to explain the *Avataṃsaka* using the *Mahāvibhāṣā*?
And do the five hundred arhats possess the same insights and understandings as the seven bodhisattvas?
The Yogācāra school differs [from this], and their similarities and differences are eternally divergent.

Regarding the phrase "Kāśyapa, you should know," since the opening verse of the *Gāthā* already stated, "You, Kāśyapa, and others should know," it is for this reason that the subsequent verses do not again emphasize or reiterate the title.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* translated by Dharmagupta during the Sui dynasty, titled the "Augmented Version" (*Tiānpǐn Fǎhuá*), followed the *Miaoběn* (Exquisite Original) for all other texts; however, upon seeing that the prose following the verses in the original manuscript contained an additional long passage of verse, he retranslated it.
After adding this passage, the "Entrusting" (*Nidāna*) chapter was moved to follow the "Exhortation" (*Pravartana*) chapter; all other previously translated sections remained unchanged.

The phrasing of the retranslation largely resembles the original text. Regarding the additions: in the initial prose section, a comparison with the sun and moon is first used to praise the Buddha’s wisdom; because this duplicates the preceding text, Master Kumārajīva did not translate it.

Next, it is explained that within the five destinies there are the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and that within these three vehicles there is taught equality; this also seems redundant with the preceding text.
Next, Kāśyapa asks: "For what reason do you bestow these teachings of the three vehicles?"
The Buddha used the analogy of earthenware vessels to illustrate this: the difference lies in what they contain, not in the clay from which they are made.
Kāśyapa asked again, "Regarding those of various understandings who have emerged beyond the triple world, are they one, two, or three?"
The Buddha replied: "If the essence of awakening is equal and there is no longer duality or plurality, this is also identical to the notion of *nirvāṇa* mentioned in the first sutra.

Subsequently, the Buddha spoke the parable of the person born blind for Kāśyapa: first, not seeing forms is likened to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); next, the opening of the eyes is likened to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*); and finally, the opening of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is likened to the Mahāyāna.
These verses are merely a reiterative recitation (geya).

Thus we know that there was no such interpolated text; the general purport is not lacking. Had there been one, it would have been redundant even if recorded. Master Kumārajīva did not translate it because he intended to avoid cumbersome prose.
Nanshan says: "Jīvaka arbitrarily moved the 'Chapter on Entrustment'. According to this, one should likewise say that he "moved the chapter [of the] Lotus Sūtra.
(Fahua Wenzuji, Scroll 7, Part 2)
